nameStory: The 'fertile' shield lichen gets its name from its readiness to produce fruiting bodies - the small, cup-like structures that hold spores for reproduction. While many lichens in this family rarely form these reproductive structures, this species is quite 'fertile' in producing them. The 'shield' part comes from the broad, flat, shield-like shape of its leafy lobes.
description: Fertile shield lichen is a leafy lichen that grows in neat rosette patterns on tree bark, looking like pale greenish-gray flowers pressed against the trunk. Each rosette can grow 6-12 cm across (about the size of your palm), with broad, overlapping lobes that radiate outward from the center. What makes this lichen special are the conspicuous pale pores scattered across its surface, which sometimes connect to form a white network pattern near the lobe tips. Unlike many of its relatives, this species frequently produces small, dark, cup-shaped fruiting bodies.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for distinctive pale pores scattered across the surface that feel slightly raised to the touch, sometimes connecting into white network patterns near the lobe tips

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms neat rosette patterns 6-12 cm across with broad, flat lobes that overlap like shingles and feel leathery when dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale greenish-gray when dry, becoming more vibrant green when wet after rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on tree bark, particularly favoring deciduous trees in coastal or humid areas

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Frequently produces small, dark, cup-shaped fruiting bodies (apothecia) that look like tiny buttons pressed into the surface

habitat: In New England, fertile shield lichen is found primarily in coastal Maine, where the maritime climate provides the humidity it needs. Look for it on the bark of deciduous trees, especially in areas influenced by ocean moisture. This is one of our rarest shield lichens, so finding it would be quite a discovery.

seasonality.spring: Fresh spring rains bring out the vibrant green colors, making the pale pores more visible against the darker wet surface.
seasonality.summer: During humid summer days, the lichen maintains good color and the fruiting bodies are most noticeable as dark spots on the surface.
seasonality.fall: Fall moisture keeps the lichen active, and this is often when new fruiting bodies develop most readily.
seasonality.winter: The lichen appears pale and grayish when dry, but the distinctive pore pattern remains visible and is actually easier to spot without competing green colors.

funFact: This lichen was hiding in plain sight in North America for over a century - originally described from Siberia in 1887, it wasn't recognized as occurring in the United States until the late 20th century when sharp-eyed lichenologists finally distinguished it from its more common relatives in Maine!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the common netted shield lichen (Parmelia sulcata), but fertile shield lichen has more prominent, paler pores and produces fruiting bodies much more readily. Memory trick: 'Fertile' makes 'fruits' (fruiting bodies) while sulcata stays sterile.
contextualKnowledge: This species shows how much we still don't know about lichen diversity - even common-looking species can turn out to be rarities that were overlooked for decades. It's a reminder that careful observation can lead to exciting discoveries, even in well-studied regions like New England.
compareHints: Among the shield lichens, fertile shield lichen is distinguished by its pale, prominent pores and frequent fruiting body production. Netted shield lichen has a more obvious white network pattern but darker, less prominent pores. Bottlebrush shield lichen has cylindrical projections rather than pores, while salted shield lichen has granular soredia instead of the smooth pored surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Netted shield lichen is distinguished from its shield lichen relatives by its unique white net pattern - bottlebrush shield lichen has tiny finger-like projections, while salted shield lichen has a more uniformly smooth surface with white spots rather than a connected network.

Bottlebrush shield lichen stands out from other Parmelia species by its distinctive branching edge projections - netted shield lichen has a more reticulated (net-like) surface pattern, while salted shield lichen has simpler, less ornate edges.
Unlike its cousin the Netted Shield Lichen which has raised white ridges forming a net pattern, Salted Shield Lichen has scattered granular patches.

Unlike Netted Shield Lichen which has a distinctly white, net-like pattern on its surface, or Bottlebrush Shield Lichen with its fuzzy, hair-like projections, Smoky Crottle has a relatively smooth surface.
